nameStory: The Lucerne Moth gets its name from one of its favorite foods - lucerne, which is another name for alfalfa (Medicago sativa). This little moth earned its common name because farmers often noticed it fluttering around their alfalfa fields, where the caterpillars munch on the nutritious crop. It's also called the 'clover nomophila' for similar reasons, as it loves various clover-family plants.
description: The Lucerne Moth is a small, brownish moth with a wingspan about the size of a quarter - roughly 1 to 1.4 inches across. It belongs to the snout moth family, though its 'snout' (actually extended mouthparts called palps) isn't as pronounced as some of its relatives. These common moths have relatively plain brown and tan coloring that helps them blend in perfectly with dried grass and soil. You'll often see them flying in a quick, erratic pattern close to the ground, especially around gardens and fields.

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning about 1 to 1.4 inches - roughly the size of a quarter when spread out

idTips.label: Wing coloration
idTips.description: Plain brownish wings with subtle tan and darker brown markings that look like dried grass - no bright colors or bold patterns

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in quick, jerky movements close to the ground, often zigzagging through low vegetation rather than soaring

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Relatively slender body for a snout moth, with modestly extended mouthparts that don't form an obvious 'snout'

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a triangular tent-like shape over its body, pressed close together

idTips.label: Habitat association
idTips.description: Almost always found near low-growing plants like clover, grasses, or garden vegetables - rarely seen far from these food sources

habitat: Look for Lucerne Moths in open, sunny areas with plenty of low-growing plants - gardens, farm fields, meadows, and grassy areas are perfect spots. They're especially common around alfalfa fields, clover patches, and vegetable gardens where celery or other herbs grow. You'll rarely find them in deep woods or areas without their preferred food plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April, flying around gardens and fields as they search for mates and egg-laying sites on young plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with multiple generations flying throughout the warm months - look for them fluttering near ground level in gardens and fields.
seasonality.fall: Still active through October and into November, with the final generation preparing for winter as caterpillars in plant debris.
seasonality.winter: No adults flying - they overwinter as caterpillars or pupae hidden in plant litter and soil.

funFact: Despite being called the 'celery stalkworm' as a caterpillar, this moth is actually more of a helpful garden visitor than a pest - the larvae usually feed on weeds and wild plants rather than destroying your prized vegetables, and the adults help pollinate small flowers as they sip nectar!
confusionNotes: Lucerne Moths are easily confused with other small brown moths, especially other members of the snout moth family. The key difference is their habitat - if you see a small brown moth flying around clover, alfalfa, or low garden plants during the day or early evening, it's likely a Lucerne Moth rather than the many similar species that prefer trees or indoor spaces.
contextualKnowledge: This moth goes by many names that can be confusing - 'false webworm' and 'celery stalkworm' refer to its caterpillar stage, while 'lucerne' is an old-fashioned name for alfalfa that's still used in some farming communities. Don't let the 'webworm' name fool you - these caterpillars don't make obvious webs like tent caterpillars do.
compareHints: The Lucerne Moth is the only Nomophila species commonly found in New England, making it easier to identify within its genus. Compared to other snout moths in the region, it's distinguished by its preference for low-growing plants rather than trees, its relatively plain brown coloring without bold stripes or spots, and its habit of flying close to the ground in open, sunny areas rather than being attracted to porch lights at night.
